title: NHC Tropical Cyclone Outlook: Rainfall & Max Sustained Wind within 500 km
text:
Every time this page is rendered (including the scheduled daily rebuild — see the note at the bottom), it:

Pulls every currently active NHC storm across the Atlantic, East Pacific, and Central Pacific basins.
For each one, downloads its official forecast track and classifies each point by Saffir-Simpson category.
Pulls matching HAFS (Hurricane Analysis and Forecast System) fields – accumulated precipitation and a period-maximum surface wind – masks each field to a 500 km circle around the storm’s forecast position at each step, sums rainfall across steps, and takes the running maximum wind seen at each pixel across the entire forecast period.
Renders one plot per storm (as a real PNG file, not an embedded image — see the caveats), and gives you a dropdown to switch between them.

The steps below are broken into the same stages, each ending with a small table or plot summarizing what that stage produced – useful both for following along and for spotting a bad storm before it reaches the final map.






Important



This dropdown does not recompute anything live. The site is static — there’s no server behind it. At render time, this code pre-computes a plot for every active storm; the dropdown just shows/hides a pre-rendered image. What you see is only as fresh as the last render (daily, via cron).

import re
import shutil
import time
import traceback
import zipfile
import io
import os
import sys
from datetime import datetime, timedelta, timezone
from pathlib import Path

# Force PROJ (used by pyproj/cartopy/fiona) to read its database from the
# conda env actually running this notebook (sys.prefix), not whatever
# PROJ_DATA/PROJ_LIB the parent shell happens to have exported -- e.g. an
# older PROJ install from a different conda env on the same machine. A
# mismatched, older proj.db raises "DATABASE.LAYOUT.VERSION.MINOR ... whereas
# a number >= 6 is expected." Must run before geopandas/pyproj/cartopy import.
os.environ["PROJ_DATA"] = os.path.join(sys.prefix, "share", "proj")
os.environ.pop("PROJ_LIB", None)

import geopandas as gpd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import requests
import xarray as xr
from matplotlib.collections import LineCollection
from matplotlib.colors import LogNorm
from matplotlib.lines import Line2D
from matplotlib.patches import Patch
from pyproj import Geod
from scipy.ndimage import gaussian_filter
import cartopy.crs as ccrs
import cartopy.feature as cfeature

# --- Configuration -----------------------------------------------------
RADIUS_KM = 500.0
BASINS = {"al": "NA", "ep": "EP", "cp": "CP"}  # NHC's own Atlantic prefix is "al"
# EXTENT_PAD_DEG is the final map's zoom level; BBOX_PAD_DEG is how far past
# that the underlying HAFS regridding domain extends, so the fetched data
# always covers a margin beyond what's actually shown (avoids a blank strip
# right at the visible edge). Keep BBOX_PAD_DEG > EXTENT_PAD_DEG by the same
# margin if you change either.
BBOX_PAD_DEG = 15.0
EXTENT_PAD_DEG = 10.0
CURRENT_STORMS_URL = "https://www.nhc.noaa.gov/CurrentStorms.json"
HAFS_MODEL = "hafsa"
HAFS_PRODUCT = "storm.atm"
HAFS_MAX_FXX = 126
GEOD = Geod(ellps="WGS84")

MM_TO_IN = 1.0 / 25.4
MPS_TO_MPH = 2.236936
ONE_MIN_SUSTAINED_FACTOR = 1.0 / 0.88  # WMO 10-min -> 1-min rule-of-thumb; not an official NHC value

# Precip colorbar: log scale so the 1-10 in range (where most of the
# interesting variation is) isn't washed out by rare, very high values.
# Capped at 30 in -- anything above renders as the top color (colorbar shows
# a ">" arrow via extend="max") rather than stretching the whole scale to
# accommodate one extreme pixel.
PRECIP_VMIN_IN = 1.0
PRECIP_VMAX_IN = 30.0

# Images are written as real PNG files (NOT embedded base64 -- Quarto's
# preview server tried to treat a base64 data: URI as a filesystem path and
# crashed with "File name too long"). RUN_TOKEN is appended as a query
# string on every <img> src so your browser can't serve a stale cached copy
# of a file that has the same name across renders.
IMAGE_DIR = Path("storm_images")
shutil.rmtree(IMAGE_DIR, ignore_errors=True)
IMAGE_DIR.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
RUN_TOKEN = int(time.time())

# Intensity-ordered warm ramp (amber -> orange -> red -> pink), least to
# most intense -- not NHC's own official category colors.
CATEGORY_COLORS = {"TD": "#FDA429", "TS": "#FB6107", "HU": "#E4003A", "MH": "#C3008F", "Unknown": "#999999"}
CATEGORY_LABELS = {
    "TD": "Tropical Depression", "TS": "Tropical Storm",
    "HU": "Hurricane (Cat 1-2)", "MH": "Major Hurricane (Cat 3+)", "Unknown": "Unknown",
}
WIND_CONTOUR_COLOR = "black"
WIND_SMOOTH_SIGMA = 3  # gaussian smoothing bandwidth, in grid cells
LAND_FILL_COLOR = "#e2e2e2"
LAND_BORDER_COLOR = "#4d4d4d"

DEBUG_RAISE = False  # False: a storm that fails at any stage below (e.g. no
                     # HAFS data yet for a brand-new invest) is skipped for
                     # the remaining stages -- reason logged as an HTML
                     # comment -- rather than taking down the whole page.
                     # Set True temporarily while chasing a specific failure
                     # to get Quarto's own full-traceback error reporting.
failures = []  # (label, traceback) pairs accumulated across every stage


def run_stage(label, fn):
    """
    Run a zero-argument callable for one storm at one pipeline stage,
    honoring DEBUG_RAISE. Returns fn()'s result, or None if this storm
    failed at this stage (and should be dropped from later stages).
    """
    try:
        return fn()
    except Exception:
        if DEBUG_RAISE:
            raise
        tb = traceback.format_exc().replace("--", "- -")
        failures.append((label, tb))
        return None


def classify_category(wind_kt):
    if wind_kt is None or (isinstance(wind_kt, float) and np.isnan(wind_kt)):
        return "Unknown"
    if wind_kt < 34:
        return "TD"
    if wind_kt < 64:
        return "TS"
    if wind_kt < 96:
        return "HU"
    return "MH"


def geodesic_circle(center_lon, center_lat, radius_km, n=72):
    az = np.linspace(0, 360, n, endpoint=True)
    lon2, lat2, _ = GEOD.fwd(np.full(n, center_lon), np.full(n, center_lat),
                              az, np.full(n, radius_km * 1000.0))
    return lon2, lat2


def circle_mask_km(lon2d, lat2d, center_lon, center_lat, radius_km):
    n = lon2d.size
    grid_lons = np.where(lon2d.ravel() > 180, lon2d.ravel() - 360, lon2d.ravel())
    _, _, dist_m = GEOD.inv(np.full(n, center_lon), np.full(n, center_lat), grid_lons, lat2d.ravel())
    return (dist_m / 1000.0 <= radius_km).reshape(lon2d.shape)


def smooth_for_contour(da, sigma=WIND_SMOOTH_SIGMA):
    """
    Gaussian-smooth a 2D field for prettier contour lines, without letting
    NaN (outside the 500 km composite footprint) bleed a false gradient into
    the valid region. Standard "fill with 0, smooth the validity mask the
    same way, divide back out" trick, then re-mask anywhere the smoothed
    validity weight is too low to trust.
    """
    values = da.values
    valid = np.isfinite(values)
    if not valid.any():
        return da
    filled = np.where(valid, values, 0.0)
    smoothed = gaussian_filter(filled, sigma=sigma)
    weight = gaussian_filter(valid.astype(float), sigma=sigma)
    with np.errstate(invalid="ignore", divide="ignore"):
        result = smoothed / weight
    result[weight < 0.2] = np.nan
    return da.copy(data=result)


def atcf_storm_id(nhc_id):
    nhc_id = nhc_id.lower()
    basin_letter = {"al": "l", "ep": "e", "cp": "c"}[nhc_id[:2]]
    return f"{nhc_id[2:4]}{basin_letter}"


def first_data_var(ds):
    skip = {"latitude", "longitude", "time", "step", "valid_time",
            "surface", "isobaricInhPa", "heightAboveGround"}
    for name in ds.data_vars:
        if name not in skip:
            return ds[name]
    raise RuntimeError(f"No data variable found in dataset: {list(ds.data_vars)}")


def best_matching_bucket(H, var_search, end_hour):
    """Widest available bucket for var_search that ends exactly at end_hour."""
    try:
        inv = H.inventory(var_search)
    except Exception:
        return None
    if inv is None or len(inv) == 0:
        return None
    pattern = re.compile(r"(\d+)-(\d+) hour")
    best, best_width = None, -1
    for _, row in inv.iterrows():
        m = pattern.search(str(row.get("forecast_time", "")))
        if not m:
            continue
        start, end = int(m.group(1)), int(m.group(2))
        if end == end_hour and (end - start) > best_width:
            best, best_width = row["search_this"], end - start
    return best

2. Load each storm’s forecast track and matching HAFS cycle


Code
from herbie import Herbie
from herbie.models.hafs import S as hafs_storms

# The HAFS cycle we pull guidance from is the same for every storm -- the
# latest 6-hourly cycle (00/06/12/18Z) that should be complete by now.
now = datetime.now(timezone.utc)
cycle_hour = (now.hour // 6) * 6
hafs_cycle = now.replace(hour=cycle_hour, minute=0, second=0, microsecond=0)
if (now - hafs_cycle) < timedelta(hours=6):
    hafs_cycle -= timedelta(hours=6)
hafs_cycle_naive = hafs_cycle.replace(tzinfo=None)


def load_track(storm):
    """Download a storm's official NHC forecast track and merge in its current position."""
    zip_url = storm["forecastTrack"]["zipFile"]
    r = requests.get(zip_url, timeout=60)
    r.raise_for_status()
    zf = zipfile.ZipFile(io.BytesIO(r.content))
    pts_candidates = [n for n in zf.namelist() if n.lower().endswith("_pts.shp")]
    if not pts_candidates:
        raise RuntimeError(f"No '*_pts.shp' in track archive for {storm['id']}")
    extract_dir = f"/tmp/nhc_track_{storm['id']}"
    zf.extractall(extract_dir)
    track_raw = gpd.read_file(f"{extract_dir}/{pts_candidates[0]}")

    tau_col = "TAU" if "TAU" in track_raw.columns else next(
        c for c in track_raw.columns if c.upper() == "TAU"
    )
    track_raw = track_raw.sort_values(tau_col).reset_index(drop=True)

    wind_col = next(
        (c for c in ["MAXWIND", "INTENSITY", "VMAX", "WIND"] if c in track_raw.columns), None
    )
    wind_kt_series = (
        track_raw[wind_col].astype(float) if wind_col else pd.Series([np.nan] * len(track_raw))
    )

    issuance = pd.to_datetime(storm["forecastTrack"]["issuance"])
    forecast_pts = pd.DataFrame({
        "tau_h": track_raw[tau_col].astype(float),
        "lon": track_raw.geometry.x,
        "lat": track_raw.geometry.y,
        "wind_kt": wind_kt_series,
    })
    forecast_pts["valid_time"] = issuance + pd.to_timedelta(forecast_pts["tau_h"], unit="h")

    init_wind_kt = pd.to_numeric(pd.Series([storm.get("intensity")]), errors="coerce").iloc[0]
    init_row = pd.DataFrame([{
        "tau_h": 0.0, "lon": storm["longitudeNumeric"], "lat": storm["latitudeNumeric"],
        "wind_kt": init_wind_kt, "valid_time": pd.to_datetime(storm["lastUpdate"]),
    }])
    track = (
        pd.concat([init_row, forecast_pts], ignore_index=True)
        .drop_duplicates(subset="tau_h").sort_values("tau_h").reset_index(drop=True)
    )
    track["category"] = track["wind_kt"].apply(classify_category)
    track["color"] = track["category"].map(CATEGORY_COLORS)

    atcf_id = atcf_storm_id(storm["id"])

    # Herbie resolves the HAFS storm-following file path by scraping NOMADS's
    # live "active storm" registry for this storm's name; a brand-new/just
    # -designated storm isn't in that registry until NOMADS/HAFS catch up,
    # and Herbie's own error for that case is an opaque AttributeError deep
    # in its HAFS template. Check for it up front with a clear message,
    # instead of every fetch in the next stage failing the same opaque way.
    if hafs_storms.id_to_name.get(atcf_id) is None:
        raise RuntimeError(
            f"HAFS has no storm-following guidance for {storm['id']} (ATCF id "
            f"'{atcf_id}') yet -- it isn't in NOMADS's active HAFS storm "
            f"registry (hafs/prod/inphfsa listing) right now. This is normal "
            f"for a storm that was just designated; it should appear once "
            f"NHC/NOMADS register it."
        )

    return {"track": track, "atcf_id": atcf_id}


storms_by_id = {}
for storm in selected_storms:
    result = run_stage(storm["dropdown_label"], lambda storm=storm: load_track(storm))
    if result is not None:
        storms_by_id[storm["id"]] = {"storm": storm, **result}

track_summary_rows = []
for entry in storms_by_id.values():
    track = entry["track"]
    if track["wind_kt"].notna().any():
        peak_category = track.loc[track["wind_kt"].idxmax(), "category"]
    else:
        peak_category = "Unknown"
    track_summary_rows.append({
        "Storm": entry["storm"]["dropdown_label"],
        "HAFS cycle": f"{hafs_cycle:%Y-%m-%d %HZ}",
        "Track points": len(track),
        "Forecast length (h)": int(track["tau_h"].max()),
        "Peak category so far": CATEGORY_LABELS[peak_category],
    })

track_summary = (
    pd.DataFrame(track_summary_rows) if track_summary_rows
    else pd.DataFrame({"note": ["No storm tracks could be loaded."]})
)

def composite_storm_fields(entry):
    """
    Fetch HAFS precip/wind for every window along the track, mask each to a
    500 km circle around that window's forecast position, and combine them:
    rainfall summed across windows, wind as the running max seen at each
    pixel across the whole forecast period.
    """
    storm, track, atcf_id = entry["storm"], entry["track"], entry["atcf_id"]

    lat_min, lat_max = track["lat"].min() - BBOX_PAD_DEG, track["lat"].max() + BBOX_PAD_DEG
    lon_min, lon_max = track["lon"].min() - BBOX_PAD_DEG, track["lon"].max() + BBOX_PAD_DEG

    # HAFS's storm.atm output is a MOVING nest -- each forecast hour's file
    # is centered on the storm's position at that hour, unlike GFS's single
    # global grid. A fixed crop can end up empty. Instead we define one
    # common target grid ourselves and interpolate every field onto it.
    target_lat = None
    target_lon = None

    def regrid_to_common(da):
        nonlocal target_lat, target_lon
        da = da.sortby("latitude").sortby("longitude")
        lon_vals = da["longitude"].values
        if lon_vals.size and lon_vals.max() > 180:
            da = da.assign_coords(longitude=(((da["longitude"] + 180) % 360) - 180)).sortby("longitude")

        if target_lat is None:
            lat_vals = da["latitude"].values
            lon_vals2 = da["longitude"].values
            lat_res = abs(float(lat_vals[1] - lat_vals[0])) if lat_vals.size > 1 else 0.05
            lon_res = abs(float(lon_vals2[1] - lon_vals2[0])) if lon_vals2.size > 1 else 0.05
            target_lat = np.arange(lat_min, lat_max, lat_res)
            target_lon = np.arange(lon_min, lon_max, lon_res)

        out = da.interp(latitude=target_lat, longitude=target_lon, method="linear")
        if bool(out.isnull().all()):
            raise RuntimeError(
                f"Regridding produced no valid data at all (target lat "
                f"[{lat_min:.2f},{lat_max:.2f}], lon [{lon_min:.2f},{lon_max:.2f}]; "
                f"native lat [{da['latitude'].values.min():.2f},{da['latitude'].values.max():.2f}], "
                f"lon [{da['longitude'].values.min():.2f},{da['longitude'].values.max():.2f}])"
            )
        return out

    def fxx_for(valid_time):
        hours = (valid_time - hafs_cycle).total_seconds() / 3600.0
        return max(int(round(hours)), 0)

    def fetch_precip_window(fxx0, fxx1):
        """
        Precip accumulated over (fxx0, fxx1] (mm). Prefers a direct HAFS
        bucket spanning exactly this window (avoids differencing two
        "since-init" cumulative fields, which assumes a fixed grid the way
        GFS has -- HAFS's nest moves, so two cumulative snapshots may not
        share the same actual coverage, and differencing them can produce
        bad values where they don't line up).
        """
        H1 = Herbie(hafs_cycle_naive, model=HAFS_MODEL, product=HAFS_PRODUCT, fxx=fxx1, storm=atcf_id, verbose=False)
        direct = best_matching_bucket(H1, ":APCP:surface:", fxx1)
        if direct is not None:
            m = re.search(r"(\d+)-(\d+) hour", direct)
            if m and int(m.group(1)) == fxx0:
                return regrid_to_common(first_data_var(H1.xarray(direct))).clip(min=0)

        a1 = regrid_to_common(first_data_var(H1.xarray(f":APCP:surface:0-{fxx1} hour acc fcst")))
        if fxx0 == 0:
            return a1.clip(min=0)
        H0 = Herbie(hafs_cycle_naive, model=HAFS_MODEL, product=HAFS_PRODUCT, fxx=fxx0, storm=atcf_id, verbose=False)
        a0 = regrid_to_common(first_data_var(H0.xarray(f":APCP:surface:0-{fxx0} hour acc fcst")))
        return (a1 - a0).clip(min=0)

    def fetch_wind_max(fxx):
        H = Herbie(hafs_cycle_naive, model=HAFS_MODEL, product=HAFS_PRODUCT, fxx=fxx, storm=atcf_id, verbose=False)
        search = best_matching_bucket(H, ":WIND:10 m above ground:", fxx)
        if search is None:
            search = f":WIND:10 m above ground:{max(fxx - 1, 0)}-{fxx} hour max fcst"
        return regrid_to_common(first_data_var(H.xarray(search)))

    precip_total = wind_running_max = lon2d = lat2d = None
    skipped_windows = []

    for i in range(1, len(track)):
        t0, t1 = track.iloc[i - 1], track.iloc[i]
        fxx0, fxx1 = fxx_for(t0["valid_time"]), fxx_for(t1["valid_time"])

        if fxx0 > HAFS_MAX_FXX or fxx1 > HAFS_MAX_FXX:
            skipped_windows.append((t0["tau_h"], t1["tau_h"], fxx0, fxx1, "beyond HAFS max lead time"))
            continue

        try:
            precip_window = fetch_precip_window(fxx0, fxx1)
            wind_window = np.fmax(fetch_wind_max(fxx0), fetch_wind_max(fxx1))
            print(f"<!-- {storm['id']} window {t0['tau_h']:.0f}h-{t1['tau_h']:.0f}h "
                  f"(fxx {fxx0}-{fxx1}): precip range "
                  f"[{float(precip_window.min()):.2f},{float(precip_window.max()):.2f}] mm, "
                  f"wind range [{float(wind_window.min()):.2f},{float(wind_window.max()):.2f}] m/s -->")
        except Exception:
            tb = traceback.format_exc().replace("--", "- -")
            skipped_windows.append((t0["tau_h"], t1["tau_h"], fxx0, fxx1, tb))
            continue

        if lon2d is None:
            lon2d, lat2d = np.meshgrid(precip_window["longitude"], precip_window["latitude"])
            precip_total = xr.zeros_like(precip_window)
            wind_running_max = xr.full_like(precip_window, np.nan)

        mask = circle_mask_km(lon2d, lat2d, t1["lon"], t1["lat"], RADIUS_KM)
        mask_da = xr.DataArray(mask, dims=precip_window.dims, coords=precip_window.coords)

        # NaN inside the mask (a target-grid pixel this window's regridded HAFS
        # nest didn't actually cover -- the moving nest doesn't sit in the same
        # place at every lead time) must be treated as "this window contributed
        # zero", not left as NaN: NaN + anything = NaN, so a single window with
        # a coverage gap at a pixel would otherwise permanently blank that pixel
        # out of the whole composite, and later lead times (more windows, more
        # nest drift) have more chances for that to happen -- this is what was
        # showing up as expanding holes in the rainfall field later in a storm's
        # life.
        precip_total = precip_total + precip_window.where(mask_da, 0).fillna(0)
        wind_masked = wind_window.where(mask_da)
        wind_running_max = xr.where(
            wind_running_max.isnull(), wind_masked, np.fmax(wind_running_max, wind_masked.fillna(-np.inf)),
        )

    if precip_total is None:
        raise RuntimeError(
            f"No windows had usable HAFS data for {storm['id']} "
            f"(all {len(skipped_windows)} window(s) skipped: {skipped_windows})"
        )
    for (tau0, tau1, fxx0, fxx1, reason) in skipped_windows:
        print(f"<!-- {storm['id']}: skipped window {tau0:.0f}h-{tau1:.0f}h (fxx {fxx0}-{fxx1}): {reason} -->")

    wind_running_max = wind_running_max.where(wind_running_max > -np.inf)

    print(f"<!-- {storm['id']} FINAL: precip total range "
          f"[{float(precip_total.min()):.2f},{float(precip_total.max()):.2f}] mm "
          f"({float(precip_total.min())*MM_TO_IN:.2f} to {float(precip_total.max())*MM_TO_IN:.2f} in) -->")

    return {
        "precip_total": precip_total,
        "wind_running_max": wind_running_max,
        "windows_used": (len(track) - 1) - len(skipped_windows),
        "windows_skipped": len(skipped_windows),
    }

def render_storm_plot(entry):
    storm, track = entry["storm"], entry["track"]
    precip_in, wind_mph = entry["precip_in"], entry["wind_mph"]

    # constrained_layout (NOT bbox_inches="tight" on savefig below) is required
    # here: cartopy's GeoAxes enforces an equal aspect ratio between its lon/lat
    # extent, and for a storm track with a much larger lat range than lon range
    # (e.g. a mostly north-south-moving storm) that shrinks the axes to a very
    # narrow column within the figure. bbox_inches="tight" then computes its
    # crop from a matplotlib/cartopy tight-bbox calculation that mishandles that
    # narrow GeoAxes and drops it entirely, leaving only the colorbar in the
    # saved PNG. constrained_layout performs the layout before draw time and
    # doesn't have this failure mode.
    fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(9, 8), subplot_kw={"projection": ccrs.PlateCarree()},
                            constrained_layout=True)

    lon_plot = xr.where(precip_in["longitude"] > 180, precip_in["longitude"] - 360, precip_in["longitude"])
    precip_plot = precip_in.where(precip_in > 0)
    mesh = ax.pcolormesh(lon_plot, precip_in["latitude"], precip_plot,
                          cmap="YlGnBu", shading="auto", transform=ccrs.PlateCarree(),
                          norm=LogNorm(vmin=PRECIP_VMIN_IN, vmax=PRECIP_VMAX_IN))
    cbar = fig.colorbar(mesh, ax=ax, orientation="vertical", pad=0.02, extend="max",
                         label="Accumulated precipitation (in)")
    cbar_ticks = [t for t in [1, 2, 3, 5, 10, 20, 30] if PRECIP_VMIN_IN <= t <= PRECIP_VMAX_IN]
    cbar.set_ticks(cbar_ticks)
    cbar.set_ticklabels([str(t) for t in cbar_ticks])

    if np.isfinite(wind_mph.values).any():
        wind_smooth = smooth_for_contour(wind_mph)
        cs = ax.contour(lon_plot, wind_smooth["latitude"], wind_smooth,
                         colors=WIND_CONTOUR_COLOR, linewidths=0.6, transform=ccrs.PlateCarree())
        ax.clabel(cs, inline=True, fontsize=7, fmt="%.0f mph")

    for _, row in track.iterrows():
        clon, clat = geodesic_circle(row["lon"], row["lat"], RADIUS_KM)
        ax.plot(clon, clat, linestyle="--", linewidth=1.0, alpha=0.7,
                color=row["color"], transform=ccrs.PlateCarree())

    if len(track) > 1:
        points = np.array([track["lon"], track["lat"]]).T.reshape(-1, 1, 2)
        segments = np.concatenate([points[:-1], points[1:]], axis=1)

    ax.scatter(track["lon"], track["lat"], c=track["color"], s=30,
               edgecolors="black", linewidths=0.5, transform=ccrs.PlateCarree(), zorder=6)

    ax.add_feature(cfeature.NaturalEarthFeature(
        "physical", "land", "50m", edgecolor="none", facecolor=LAND_FILL_COLOR), zorder=0)
    ax.add_feature(cfeature.NaturalEarthFeature(
        "physical", "coastline", "50m", edgecolor=LAND_BORDER_COLOR, facecolor="none"), linewidth=1.2, zorder=1)
    ax.add_feature(cfeature.NaturalEarthFeature(
        "cultural", "admin_0_boundary_lines_land", "50m", edgecolor=LAND_BORDER_COLOR, facecolor="none"),
        linewidth=0.8, zorder=1)

    ax.set_extent([
        track["lon"].min() - EXTENT_PAD_DEG, track["lon"].max() + EXTENT_PAD_DEG,
        track["lat"].min() - EXTENT_PAD_DEG, track["lat"].max() + EXTENT_PAD_DEG,
    ], crs=ccrs.PlateCarree())

    gl = ax.gridlines(draw_labels=True, linewidth=0.3, color="gray", alpha=0.6, linestyle="--")
    try:
        gl.top_labels = False
        gl.right_labels = False
    except AttributeError:
        gl.xlabels_top = False
        gl.ylabels_right = False

    ax.set_title(
        f"{storm['name']} ({storm['id'].upper()}) — advisory "
        f"{storm['forecastTrack']['advNum']} — HAFS-A {hafs_cycle:%Y-%m-%d %HZ}"
    )

    present_categories = [c for c in ["TD", "TS", "HU", "MH"] if c in track["category"].values]
    legend_handles = [
        Line2D([0], [0], color=CATEGORY_COLORS[c], lw=2.5, label=CATEGORY_LABELS[c])
        for c in present_categories

    legend_handles.append(Patch(facecolor="#3f7fae", label="Rainfall accumulation (fill, in)"))
    legend_handles.append(Line2D([0], [0], color=WIND_CONTOUR_COLOR, lw=0.6,
                                  label="Max sustained wind, ~1-min (contours, mph)"))
    legend_handles.append(Line2D([0], [0], color="gray", lw=1.0, linestyle="--", label="500 km radius"))
    ax.legend(handles=legend_handles, loc="lower left", fontsize=7.5)

    # --- save as a real file (not embedded base64) ----------------------

    fig.savefig(image_path, format="png", dpi=140)
    plt.close(fig)

    return {"slug": slug, "label": storm["dropdown_label"], "img_path": image_path.as_posix()}

section: Method notes & caveats
text:
Method notes & caveats

Images are real PNG files, not embedded base64. An earlier version embedded each plot as a data:image/png;base64,... URI directly in the page. Quarto’s preview dev server tried to resolve that string as a filesystem path and crashed with File name too long. Files are now written to storm_images/ next to this post and referenced by a normal relative path, with a ?v=<timestamp> query string appended so your browser can’t serve a stale cached copy of a file that has the same name across renders — worth knowing about if you ever see an old plot persist despite a successful re-render.
Multi-basin labels: NHC’s own id prefix for the Atlantic is al; we display it as NA per your request, but filter on al internally.
Why HAFS, not HRRR: HRRR’s CONUS-only domain has no data for Central Pacific storms and misses most of the deep tropics. HAFS is NHC’s own storm-following hurricane model and covers all three basins.
HAFS’s moving nest: unlike GFS’s single global grid, every forecast hour’s HAFS file is centered on the storm’s position at that hour. A fixed-box crop (which worked fine for GFS) can end up empty. This code instead defines one common target grid and .interp()s every field onto it, and prints a per-window <!-- ... precip range ... --> diagnostic comment (visible in the page’s HTML source) so a bad window is easy to spot rather than silently producing an empty or wildly-out-of-range result.
Precip windowing: prefers a direct HAFS bucket spanning exactly the needed window; falls back to differencing two cumulative fields only if no direct match exists (differencing across a moving nest is the more fragile of the two approaches).
“1-minute sustained” wind: HAFS’s wind field is a model wind, not NHC’s official 1-minute convention. The ÷0.88 factor is a standard WMO approximation, not an official NHC intensity estimate.
DEBUG_RAISE = False: a storm that fails at any stage (e.g. no HAFS storm-following guidance published yet for a brand-new invest) is dropped from the remaining stages, with the reason logged as an HTML comment in the page source, rather than taking down the whole page. Flip it to True temporarily while chasing a specific failure to get Quarto’s own full-traceback error reporting instead.
Herbie’s own console output is suppressed (Herbie(..., verbose=False)) – by default it prints a ✅ Found ┊ ... line for every GRIB/IDX file it checks, which is useful interactively but was showing up as raw, ANSI-coded noise in this page’s rendered output. The per-window <!-- ... --> diagnostic comments above are this page’s own, deliberately HTML-commented-out replacement.
PROJ_DATA is set explicitly at the top of the setup cell, pointed at the running Python environment’s own PROJ install (sys.prefix). Without this, a PROJ_DATA/PROJ_LIB variable inherited from the shell (e.g. pointing at an older PROJ install in a different conda env) can make pyproj/cartopy/fiona load a mismatched, too-old proj.db and fail with a DATABASE.LAYOUT.VERSION.MINOR error.
First real run: check the per-window precip/wind range comments in the page source (or terminal) first if anything looks wrong — they’ll show exactly which window (if any) is producing bad numbers, rather than only seeing the final aggregate.

text:
Every time this page is rendered (once a month — see the note at the bottom), it:

Takes a fixed list of the 50 most populous US cities (a standard proxy for “most influential” — see the caveats section for why population, not some other ranking, was used).
For each city, finds the most complete nearby weather station (the candidate with the longest history and the best coverage of the target month, not just the closest one).
Compares every day of that station’s history against the all-time record for that calendar day — separately for daily highs and daily lows — using an expanding, backward-looking record: a record broken in one year moves the bar for every later year, and never the reverse (see the methodology note and worked example below).
Keeps a running tally since 2020 for both highs and lows, broken out by year.
Focuses on the most recently fully-completed calendar month and, for each city, counts how many days that month landed in each band relative to its record high and its record low — then maps both.







Important



This is a live, self-refreshing page, not a one-time snapshot. There’s no server behind it — it’s a static site. At render time, this code re-fetches real station data and recomputes everything below. What you see is only as fresh as the last render (monthly, via cron — see the bottom of the page).

Every time this page is rendered (once a month — see the note at the bottom), it:

Takes a fixed list of the 50 most populous US cities (a standard proxy for “most influential” — see the caveats section for why population, not some other ranking, was used).
For each city, finds the most complete nearby weather station (the candidate with the longest history and the best coverage of the target month, not just the closest one).

Keeps a running tally since 2020 for both highs and lows, broken out by year.
Focuses on the most recently fully-completed calendar month and, for each city, counts how many days that month landed in each band relative to its record high and its record low — then maps both.

This is a live, self-refreshing page, not a one-time snapshot. There’s no server behind it — it’s a static site. Fetched in parallel — each station’s history is an independent network call, and there’s no reason to wait for one before starting the next.

def fetch_station_tmax(station_id):
    ts = meteostat.daily(station_id, HIST_START, FETCH_END, parameters=[Parameter.TMAX])
    df = ts.fetch(units=UnitSystem.IMPERIAL)
    if df is None or df.empty:
        return None
    return df["tmax"].dropna()


# Fetch every candidate for every city (not just the nearest one) so the
# best-populated station can be picked rather than just the closest one
# that clears a minimum bar. This matters: nearby() returns candidates by
# *distance*, and the physically closest site is sometimes a short-lived or
# sparsely-reporting station (e.g. a personal/community site) sitting right
# next to a much longer-running official airport station a few km further
# out. Picking "nearest that passes" over "most complete overall" was
# initially producing "records" built on a couple sparse decades instead of
# a station's full, well-populated history.

station_series = {}
with ThreadPoolExecutor(max_workers=N_WORKERS) as pool:
    futures = {pool.submit(fetch_station_tmax, sid): sid for sid in all_candidate_ids}
    for future in futures:
        sid = futures[future]
        station_series[sid] = run_stage(f"station {sid} (fetch)", future.result)


MONTH_DATES = pd.date_range(TARGET_MONTH_START, TARGET_MONTH_END, freq="D")


def resolve_city(label, candidates):
    """
    Among this city's already-fetched candidate stations, pick whichever
    has the most actual years of history (not just whichever is nearest),
    is recent enough, and covers enough of the target month. Returns None
    (city dropped, reason logged) if none qualify.
    """
    reasons = []
    scored = []
    for station_id in candidates:
        series = station_series.get(station_id)
        if series is None or series.empty:
            reasons.append(f"{station_id}: no data returned")
            continue

        n_years = series.index.year.nunique()
        if n_years < MIN_RECORD_YEARS:
            reasons.append(f"{station_id}: only {n_years} year(s) of history")
            continue

        latest_available = series.index.max().date()
        if (TARGET_MONTH_END - latest_available).days > MAX_STALENESS_DAYS:
            reasons.append(
                f"{station_id}: most recent reading ({latest_available}) is more "
                f"than {MAX_STALENESS_DAYS} days before month-end {TARGET_MONTH_END}"
            )
            continue

        coverage = series.index.normalize().isin(MONTH_DATES).sum() / len(MONTH_DATES)
        if coverage < MIN_MONTH_COVERAGE:
            reasons.append(
                f"{station_id}: only {coverage:.0%} of {TARGET_MONTH_START:%B %Y} covered "
                f"(need {MIN_MONTH_COVERAGE:.0%})"
            )
            continue

        scored.append((n_years, station_id, series))

    if not scored:
        raise RuntimeError(f"No usable candidate station for {label}: " + "; ".join(reasons))

    # Most years of history wins, not nearest distance.
    n_years, station_id, series = max(scored, key=lambda t: t[0])
    return {"station": station_id, "n_years": n_years, "series": series}


results = {}
with ThreadPoolExecutor(max_workers=N_WORKERS) as pool:
    futures = {
        pool.submit(resolve_city, label, city_candidates[label]): label
        for name, state, lat, lon in CITIES
        for label in [f"{name}, {state}"]
    }
    for future in futures:
        label = futures[future]
        result = run_stage(label, future.result)
        if result is not None:
            results[label] = result

title: How Close Did Your City Come to a Temperature Record Last Month? Tracking 50 Major US Cities
section: Method notes & caveats
text:
Method notes & caveats

“50 most influential cities” = 50 most populous cities. Population (~2023-2024 Census estimates) is used as a standard, reproducible proxy for “influential” — there’s no single agreed-upon ranking for the latter, and population is the one that’s citable and doesn’t change based on opinion. Dallas/Fort Worth/Arlington originally plotted three overlapping points in one metro area; trimmed to just Dallas. Oakland (already effectively covered by San Francisco/San Jose in the same Bay Area), Long Beach, Fresno, Mesa, and Baltimore were swapped for Billings MT, Boise ID, Sioux Falls SD, New Orleans LA, Salt Lake City UT, Birmingham AL (the most populous of Birmingham/Mobile AL/Jackson MS), and St. Louis MO — trading a few duplicated/nearby metros for broader geographic spread.
Data source: Meteostat, which aggregates NOAA/NWS (and other) station daily summaries. Station histories vary in length — some (e.g. long-running first-order airports) go back 80+ years; others considerably less. This is each station’s own digitized daily record, not necessarily an official NWS all-time record for that city (which may rely on a longer or differently-sourced period of record).
Why monthly, not daily: a single day is a noisy, low-signal snapshot, and daily reruns mostly re-fetched the same station histories for a one-day-later answer. Rendering once a month for the prior, fully completed month gives station data real time to finalize (some long-running stations lag by a week or more — see the staleness note below) and produces a more meaningful “how hot/cold did this month actually run” summary than a single day ever could.
Highs and lows share one mechanism, mirrored. expanding_daily_comparison() takes a mode argument (“max” for daily highs, “min” for daily lows) and internally flips the sign of diff_f for the “min” case, so that diff_f > 0 always means “this day set a new record in the extreme direction” regardless of which one is being computed. classify_diff() and classify_month() are likewise shared by both — only the color/label tables (MONTH_TIERS vs. MONTH_TIERS_MIN) and the category names (“Above record” vs. “Below record”) differ.
Station choice picks the most complete candidate, not the nearest one. Up to 5 candidates within 120 km are fetched for each city, and whichever has the most actual years of daily-high history is used — not whichever is physically closest. This was a deliberate fix after an initial version picked the nearest station unconditionally (as long as it cleared MIN_RECORD_YEARS), which for at least one test city turned out to be a nearby short/sparsely-reporting site instead of a much longer-running official airport station a few km further out. The same station (and thus the same daily-low series) is used for both the high-temperature and low-temperature analyses, rather than running two independent searches that could disagree.
A candidate station must also cover the target month. Beyond overall history length, MIN_MONTH_COVERAGE (80%) requires a candidate to have data for most of the target month specifically — a station can have decades of history and still have gone offline (or not yet reported) for the one month this page currently cares about.
Reporting lag / staleness: some stations’ daily summaries aren’t finalized for a couple of weeks. A candidate is rejected if its most recent reading is more than 21 days behind the target month’s end — generous on purpose, since the long-running official stations that make the best record sources also tend to have the slowest final QC lag.
A calendar day’s record also needs a minimum sample size of its own (MIN_PRIOR_SAMPLES = 15 earlier years). A station can pass the overall history-length bar while a specific month/day within it still has very few prior observations early in the record, making that day’s “record” trivially easy to beat — this floor keeps those thin spots out of every tally on this page.
The multi-year tallies and monthly maps use an expanding, backward-looking record. Comparing every day against the extreme over all years, including ones after it, would let e.g. a hot day in 2024 count as “the record” a 2020 reading is judged against, which reverses cause and effect. Instead, each day is compared only to the most extreme reading ever seen on that calendar day in a strictly earlier year, so a new record set in one year correctly moves the bar for every year after it, and never for years before it — see the worked spot-check in section 3, which finds a real (city, day) example and shows the record baseline actually changing over time rather than just asserting it does.
“Tied” means ±0.5°F, not ±1°F. An earlier version of this page used a ±1°F band (diff_f >= -1) for the “tied” tally category, which is a 2°F-wide window, not the 1°F-wide “within a degree” that was actually intended. TIED_BAND_F = 0.5 fixes this: “at record (tied)” now means -0.5 <= diff_f <= 0.5, a 1°F-wide band centered on the record.
Why this color ladder (and why it’s not literally the first draft): it went through a few rounds. The very first version had two buckets defined identically (“< 3 days within 3°F” listed twice). The settled version is a 9-step diverging ladder: two fully-saturated anchor colors at the extremes, shading through progressively lighter tones toward a neutral gray in the middle, with each of the “tied” / “within 3°F” / “within 10°F” bands split into its own “3+ days” and “1-2 days” tier (checked 3+ first, so a city with 3+ days never gets miscounted into the “1-2” tier just because 1-2 is also technically true). One asymmetry worth calling out: the bottom tier’s label (“At least 1 day within 10°F”) is a holdover from before the “3+ days within 10°F” tier existed just above it — in practice that tier only ever fires for 1-2 days now, since 3+ is claimed first, but the exact wording wasn’t revisited.
Daily lows use the same ladder shape with the colors deliberately inverted. For daily highs, red means “notably hot” (close to or beyond the record) and blue means “far from the hot record, i.e. a relatively cool month.” For daily lows, blue instead means “notably cold” (close to or beyond the record low) and red means “far from the cold record, i.e. a relatively mild month” — matching the intuitive association of blue with cold and red with warm, at the cost of the two maps not sharing one universal color meaning (check each map’s own legend).
Why 2020 for the multi-year tally: 2020 was chosen as a round, recent starting point with enough span to show a year-over-year pattern rather than just one data point; there’s nothing special about that year beyond that.
DEBUG_RAISE = False: a city that fails at any stage (no usable station, insufficient history, stale data, insufficient month coverage, or — for the low-temperature analysis specifically — a station that reports highs but not lows) is dropped, with the reason logged as an HTML comment in the page source, rather than taking down the whole page. Flip it to True temporarily to get a full traceback while debugging a specific city.
Large-request guard disabled on purpose: Meteostat blocks any single daily-data request spanning more than 30 years by default. That’s turned off here (meteostat.config.block_large_requests = False) deliberately, since computing an honest “record for this calendar day” requires each station’s entire digitized history, not just the last 30 years.
Station fetches run in parallel (ThreadPoolExecutor, up to 10 at once) since each is an independent network call to Meteostat’s bulk data. Every candidate for every city is fetched (not just the nearest one, per the station-choice note above), so this stage pulls roughly 5x more station histories than there are cities — still well worth parallelizing, but it’s the long pole in this page’s render time (on the order of 15-20 minutes for all 50 cities). That’s a real cost, but at a monthly cadence it’s a non-issue.

section: 3. Back-calculated running tally since 2020
text:
3. Back-calculated running tally since 2020
A single month is a small sample — most cities aren’t near their record in any given month. To get a real sense of how often major US cities are running hot relative to their own history, this section replays the comparison for every day since datetime.date(2020, 1, 1) through the end of the target month, for each of the 50 resolved cities (using the station histories already pulled above — no extra fetching needed), and keeps a cumulative tally across all of it. The per-day results computed here also feed directly into the monthly map in the next section.
The one thing that has to change for a multi-year replay: “the record” can’t be a fixed number looked up once, because it should only reflect what was actually the record at the time — a day in 2021 should be judged against the record as it stood coming into 2021, not against a hotter day that happened to occur in 2023. So for each station and each calendar day, this uses an expanding, backward-looking record: the highest reading ever seen on that calendar day in any earlier year. If a year sets a new record, that becomes the bar every later year is compared against — and, just as importantly, a year never gets compared against a record set after it.


Code
def expanding_daily_comparison(series):
    """
    For one station's full daily-tmax series, return a DataFrame (one row
    per date) with each day's reading compared against the expanding,
    backward-looking record for that calendar day -- i.e. the max reading
    ever seen on that month/day in a *strictly earlier* year.

    Rows where fewer than MIN_PRIOR_SAMPLES earlier years exist for that
    calendar day are dropped, not just rows with zero prior years. A
    station can pass the overall MIN_RECORD_YEARS bar and still have a
    calendar day's "record" resting on only a handful of early
    observations -- comparing against a record that immature makes it
    trivially easy to "beat," which would inflate every tally below with
    noise rather than genuine extremes.
    """
    df = series.rename("actual_f").to_frame()
    df["month"] = df.index.month
    df["day"] = df.index.day
    grouped = df.groupby(["month", "day"])["actual_f"]
    df["prior_record_f"] = grouped.transform(lambda s: s.expanding().max().shift(1))
    df["prior_n"] = grouped.transform(lambda s: s.expanding().count().shift(1))
    df = df[df["prior_n"] >= MIN_PRIOR_SAMPLES]
    df["diff_f"] = (df["actual_f"] - df["prior_record_f"]).round(1)
    return df[["actual_f", "prior_record_f", "diff_f"]]


daily_frames = []
for label, r in results.items():
    comparison = run_stage(f"{label} (historical replay)",
                            lambda r=r: expanding_daily_comparison(r["series"]))
    if comparison is None:
        continue
    comparison = comparison.loc[TALLY_START_DATE:TARGET_MONTH_END].copy()
    comparison["City"] = label
    daily_frames.append(comparison)

daily_tally_df = pd.concat(daily_frames)
daily_tally_df["Tally category"] = daily_tally_df["diff_f"].apply(tally_category)

daily_tally_df["month"] = daily_tally_df.index.month
daily_tally_df["day"] = daily_tally_df.index.day

overall_tally = (
    daily_tally_df["Tally category"].value_counts().reindex(TALLY_CATEGORIES, fill_value=0)
)
overall_tally_table = (
    overall_tally.rename("City-days").reset_index().rename(columns={"index": "Category"})

2. Pull each station’s full daily high/low-temperature history
Fetched in parallel — each station’s history is an independent network call, and there’s no reason to wait for one before starting the next. Both the daily high and daily low come back in the same request per station, so adding the low-temperature analysis below didn’t require any extra fetching.


Code
def fetch_station_daily(station_id):
    ts = meteostat.daily(station_id, HIST_START, FETCH_END, parameters=[Parameter.TMAX, Parameter.TMIN])
    return ts.fetch(units=UnitSystem.IMPERIAL)


# Fetch every candidate for every city (not just the nearest one) so the
# best-populated station can be picked rather than just the closest one
# that clears a minimum bar. This matters: nearby() returns candidates by
# *distance*, and the physically closest site is sometimes a short-lived or
# sparsely-reporting station (e.g. a personal/community site) sitting right
# next to a much longer-running official airport station a few km further
# out. Picking "nearest that passes" over "most complete overall" was
# initially producing "records" built on a couple sparse decades instead of
# a station's full, well-populated history.
all_candidate_ids = sorted({sid for ids in city_candidates.values() for sid in ids})
station_data = {}
with ThreadPoolExecutor(max_workers=N_WORKERS) as pool:
    futures = {pool.submit(fetch_station_daily, sid): sid for sid in all_candidate_ids}
    for future in futures:
        sid = futures[future]
        station_data[sid] = run_stage(f"station {sid} (fetch)", future.result)


MONTH_DATES = pd.date_range(TARGET_MONTH_START, TARGET_MONTH_END, freq="D")


def resolve_city(label, candidates):
    """
    Among this city's already-fetched candidate stations, pick whichever
    has the most actual years of daily-high history (not just whichever is
    nearest), is recent enough, and covers enough of the target month.
    Station choice is driven entirely by the high-temperature series --
    a station reporting both highs and lows normally has matching coverage
    for both, so this avoids running two separate (and possibly
    conflicting) candidate searches. Returns None (city dropped, reason
    logged) if no candidate qualifies.
    """
    reasons = []
    scored = []
    for station_id in candidates:
        df = station_data.get(station_id)
        if df is None or df.empty or "tmax" not in df.columns:
            reasons.append(f"{station_id}: no data returned")
            continue

        tmax_series = df["tmax"].dropna()
        if tmax_series.empty:
            reasons.append(f"{station_id}: no daily-high data returned")
            continue

        n_years = tmax_series.index.year.nunique()
        if n_years < MIN_RECORD_YEARS:
            reasons.append(f"{station_id}: only {n_years} year(s) of history")
            continue

        latest_available = tmax_series.index.max().date()
        if (TARGET_MONTH_END - latest_available).days > MAX_STALENESS_DAYS:
            reasons.append(
                f"{station_id}: most recent reading ({latest_available}) is more "
                f"than {MAX_STALENESS_DAYS} days before month-end {TARGET_MONTH_END}"
            )
            continue

        coverage = tmax_series.index.normalize().isin(MONTH_DATES).sum() / len(MONTH_DATES)
        if coverage < MIN_MONTH_COVERAGE:
            reasons.append(
                f"{station_id}: only {coverage:.0%} of {TARGET_MONTH_START:%B %Y} covered "
                f"(need {MIN_MONTH_COVERAGE:.0%})"
            )
            continue

        tmin_series = df["tmin"].dropna() if "tmin" in df.columns else pd.Series(dtype=float)
        scored.append((n_years, station_id, tmax_series, tmin_series))

    if not scored:
        raise RuntimeError(f"No usable candidate station for {label}: " + "; ".join(reasons))

    # Most years of high-temp history wins, not nearest distance.
    n_years, station_id, tmax_series, tmin_series = max(scored, key=lambda t: t[0])
    return {
        "station": station_id, "n_years": n_years,
        "tmax_series": tmax_series, "tmin_series": tmin_series,
    }


results = {}
with ThreadPoolExecutor(max_workers=N_WORKERS) as pool:
    futures = {
        pool.submit(resolve_city, label, city_candidates[label]): label
        for name, state, lat, lon in CITIES
        for label in [f"{name}, {state}"]
    }
    for future in futures:
        label = futures[future]
        result = run_stage(label, future.result)
        if result is not None:
            results[label] = result

print(f"Resolved {len(results)} / {len(CITIES)} cities for {TARGET_MONTH_START:%B %Y}.")
if failures:
    print(f"{len(failures)} city/stage combination(s) failed -- see HTML source comments for details.")

def expanding_daily_comparison(series, mode="max"):
    """
    For one station's full daily series (highs or lows), return a
    DataFrame (one row per date) with each day's reading compared against
    the expanding, backward-looking record for that calendar day -- i.e.
    the most extreme reading ever seen on that month/day in a *strictly
    earlier* year.

    mode="max" is for daily highs (record = highest prior reading);
    mode="min" is for daily lows (record = lowest prior reading, and the
    sign of diff_f is flipped so that diff_f > 0 always means "this day
    set a new record," regardless of mode -- callers never need to know
    which mode produced a given diff_f.

    Rows where fewer than MIN_PRIOR_SAMPLES earlier years exist for that
    calendar day are dropped, not just rows with zero prior years. A
    station can pass the overall MIN_RECORD_YEARS bar and still have a
    calendar day's "record" resting on only a handful of early
    observations -- comparing against a record that immature makes it
    trivially easy to "beat," which would inflate every tally below with
    noise rather than genuine extremes.
    """
    df = series.rename("actual_f").to_frame()
    df["month"] = df.index.month
    df["day"] = df.index.day
    grouped = df.groupby(["month", "day"])["actual_f"]
    df["prior_n"] = grouped.transform(lambda s: s.expanding().count().shift(1))
    if mode == "max":
        df["prior_record_f"] = grouped.transform(lambda s: s.expanding().max().shift(1))
    else:
        df["prior_record_f"] = grouped.transform(lambda s: s.expanding().min().shift(1))
    df = df[df["prior_n"] >= MIN_PRIOR_SAMPLES]
    if mode == "max":
        df["diff_f"] = (df["actual_f"] - df["prior_record_f"]).round(1)
    else:
        df["diff_f"] = (df["prior_record_f"] - df["actual_f"]).round(1)
    return df[["actual_f", "prior_record_f", "diff_f"]]

3. Back-calculated running tally since 2020 — daily highs
A single month is a small sample — most cities aren’t near their record in any given month. To get a real sense of how often major US cities are running hot relative to their own history, this section replays the comparison for every day since datetime.date(2020, 1, 1) through the end of the target month, for each of the 50 resolved cities (using the station histories already pulled above — no extra fetching needed), and keeps a cumulative tally across all of it. The per-day results computed here also feed directly into the monthly map in section 5.
The one thing that has to change for a multi-year replay: “the record” can’t be a fixed number looked up once, because it should only reflect what was actually the record at the time — a day in 2021 should be judged against the record as it stood coming into 2021, not against a hotter day that happened to occur in 2023. So for each station and each calendar day, this uses an expanding, backward-looking record: the highest reading ever seen on that calendar day in any earlier year. If a year sets a new record, that becomes the bar every later year is compared against — and, just as importantly, a year never gets compared against a record set after it.

The inverse of section 3: the same expanding, backward-looking-record mechanism, applied to each station’s daily low instead of daily high. “The record” here is the coldest reading ever seen on that calendar day in a strictly earlier year, and a day “sets a new record” by coming in colder than that – everything else about the methodology (minimum prior sample size, never letting a later year’s cold snap count against an earlier year, TIED_BAND_F for “tied”) is identical to the high-temperature version above.
